# Compactness on a fixed projection with an interior lattice fiber

## The statement

Fix d>=1 and a finite lattice-convex set P in Z^n, meaning
P=conv(P) intersect Z^n. Fix z_0 in P lying in the relative interior of
conv(P). For each member of a family let

    C = conv union_(z in P) ({z} x K_z),

where the K_z are nonempty compact convex subsets of R^d, and assume they
are the actual fibers of C at z. Suppose K_(z_0) has positive d-volume.

After maps of the form

    (z,x) -> (z, A x+Bz+b),       A in GL(d,R),

the entire family has all its fibers in one fixed Euclidean ball whose
radius depends only on P and d. Thus it is precompact in the product of the
Hausdorff topologies of the finitely many fibers. If |K_(z_0)|=1 initially,
the maps can be chosen with det(A)=1. If, in addition,

    0<ell <= |K_z| <= u<infinity

for every z and every member, the limit fibers remain full-dimensional and
the limit family remains an actual convex fiber family with projection P.
The normalized maximum halfspace depth is continuous along such normalized
convergent families. This continuity remains true without the other-fiber
volume bounds, allowing zero-volume limit fibers; the central fiber keeps
volume one.

In fact the upper and lower volume bounds on the OTHER fibers are not needed
for boundedness. They are needed only when EVERY fiber is required to remain positive-volume
in a limit. The interior-fiber hypothesis is essential to the proof;
no claim is made here for hollow P.

All the transformations preserve Z^n x R^d bijectively. They multiply every
fiber d-volume, and hence mixed volume, by the same |det(A)|; halfspaces map
to halfspaces. Thus normalized halfspace depth is unchanged.

## 1. A self-contained volume-preserving normalization of one fiber

First normalize |K_(z_0)|=1 by a common scalar map if necessary. This does
not change any normalized depth. If the original volumes are in [ell,u],
after this preliminary step they are in [ell/u,u/ell].

Here is an elementary alternative to invoking John's ellipsoid theorem.
Choose a maximum-volume inscribed d-simplex in K_(z_0), which exists by
compactness and has positive volume. Affinely send its vertices to
0,e_1,...,e_d. Call the linear part A_0 and its absolute determinant D.
Replacing vertex i of this simplex by any point x of the transformed body
multiplies simplex volume by the absolute value of the ith barycentric
coordinate of x. Maximality therefore says every barycentric coordinate
has absolute value at most one. In particular the body is contained in
[-1,1]^d and contains the standard simplex. Consequently

    1/d! <= D <= 2^d,

because its original volume was one. Translate the standard simplex's
barycenter to the origin, and then multiply by D^(-1/d). The resulting linear
map has absolute determinant one (an optional reflection makes it positive).
The normalized central fiber contains rho B_d and is contained in R B_d,
where one valid choice is

    rho = 1/[2(d+1)sqrt(d)],
    R   = 2 sqrt(d) (d!)^(1/d).

Indeed the standard simplex contains the ball of radius
1/[(d+1)sqrt(d)] about its barycenter, while the translated cube lies in the
ball of radius 2sqrt(d). The displayed determinant bounds give the stated
radii. Only the outer radius R will be used for boundedness.

Alternatively, volume-preserving John normalization gives the better radii
rho=kappa_d^(-1/d)/d and R=d kappa_d^(-1/d), where kappa_d is unit-ball volume.
The elementary normalization above makes the present proof independent of
that named theorem.

## 2. Fixed positive barycentric weights bound all diameters

There are fixed numbers p_z>0, depending only on P and z_0, such that

    sum_z p_z=1,      sum_z p_z z=z_0.

For example let bar_z be the average of all points of P. Since z_0 is in
relative interior, for sufficiently small theta>0 one can write
z_0=theta bar_z+(1-theta)y with y in conv(P). Expanding y as a convex
combination and adding theta/|P| to each coefficient gives the required
strictly positive weights. This also works if conv(P) is lower-dimensional.

Actual-fiber compatibility and convexity imply the Minkowski inclusion

    sum_z p_z K_z subset K_(z_0).

Widths add under Minkowski sums. Hence, for every unit vector u,

    p_z width(K_z,u) <= width(K_(z_0),u) <= 2R.

Taking the supremum over u yields the explicit bounds

    diam(K_z) <= 2R/p_z.

These bounds are unaffected by translating individual fibers. They required
no lower or upper bound on their volumes.

## 3. An affine shear bounds every center displacement

Let r=dim aff(P), and choose z_1,...,z_r in P so that z_i-z_0 are independent.
Choose centers c_i in K_(z_i) arbitrarily, and use c_0=0 in the normalized
central fiber. There is a linear map B on R^n satisfying

    B(z_i-z_0)=c_i,       1<=i<=r.

Its values off the span of these vectors can be arbitrary. Apply the fiber
shear x -> x-B(z-z_0). After this shear the chosen points in the basis fibers
are all zero, and the central fiber has not changed. In every other fiber
choose any point c_z of the sheared fiber.

For a nonbasis z, write its unique affine coordinates

    z=lambda_0 z_0+sum_(i=1)^r lambda_i z_i,
    lambda_0+sum_i lambda_i=1.

Define the fixed affine-dependence vector a^(z) on P by coefficient +1 at z,
coefficient -lambda_i at z_i (including i=0), and zero elsewhere. Set

    epsilon_z = min_(w:a_w^(z)!=0) p_w/[2|a_w^(z)|] > 0.

Both vectors p+epsilon_z a^(z) and p-epsilon_z a^(z) have positive
coefficients, sum one, and have integer-coordinate barycenter z_0. Applying
convexity to the chosen centers shows that

    sum_w p_w c_w + epsilon_z c_z,
    sum_w p_w c_w - epsilon_z c_z

both belong to K_(z_0), which is contained in R B_d. Their difference gives

    |c_z| <= R/epsilon_z.

For the basis centers c_z=0. Combining this with the diameter bound gives

    K_z subset [R/epsilon_z+2R/p_z] B_d

for each nonbasis z, and K_(z_i) subset (2R/p_(z_i)) B_d for the basis
fibers (the central fiber has the stronger radius R). All constants depend
only on P and d. If P={z_0}, the earlier one-fiber normalization suffices.

This proves the claimed bound on nonaffine center displacements, not merely
on the diameters of the fibers. Unbounded affine displacements have been
removed by the single admissible shear.

## 4. Limits preserve actual-fiber compatibility

The uniformly bounded nonempty convex fibers have a simultaneous Hausdorff
convergent subsequence by the elementary compactness theorem for bounded
compact convex sets. Denote their limits by K_z^infinity and put

    C_infinity=conv union_z ({z} x K_z^infinity).

The convex hulls converge in Hausdorff distance, and their projection is
conv(P). To verify that the actual fiber at an integer z in P is exactly
K_z^infinity, take any (z,x) in C_infinity. Since P is finite and each fiber
is convex, it can be written

    (z,x)=sum_w lambda_w (w,x_w),
    lambda_w>=0, sum_w lambda_w=1, x_w in K_w^infinity.

Choose approximations x_w^j in K_w^j. The SAME coefficients give
(z,sum_w lambda_w x_w^j) in C_j. Its integer coordinate is exactly z, so its
continuous coordinate belongs to the original actual fiber K_z^j. Passing
to the limit gives x in K_z^infinity. The reverse inclusion is immediate.
There are no extra integer projection points because P is lattice-convex.

Volume is continuous under Hausdorff convergence of compact convex sets.
The volume-preserving normalization after |K_(z_0)|=1 leaves the bounds
unchanged, so all limiting fibers retain their stipulated positive lower
volume bound. The limit central fiber also has volume one and contains
rho B_d. When aff(P)=R^n, C_infinity is full-dimensional in R^(n+d): an
interior ball in one fiber and an affine basis of projection fibers span
the full dimension.

## 5. Continuity of normalized maximum depth

Let all normalized fibers lie in a common ball of radius R_*.
Hausdorff convergence of convex bodies gives convergence of their indicator
functions in L^1. For a full-dimensional limit, its boundary has Lebesgue
measure zero, and interior/exterior points eventually retain their membership;
dominated convergence applies in the fixed common ball. For a lower-dimensional
limit, its d-volume is zero and volume continuity directly gives L^1 convergence
to its zero-almost-everywhere indicator. Thus this step does not need any
positive lower bound on the noncentral fibers.
Therefore the finite sums of fiber Lebesgue measures converge in total
variation. Write these measures as mu_j and mu_infinity, with masses M_j and
M_infinity>0.

There is also a uniform continuity estimate for moving a candidate within
one integer fiber. A containing halfspace can always be moved inward until
its boundary contains the candidate. Write such a halfspace through (z,x) as

    a.(w-z)+u.(y-x)>=0.

If u=0, replacing x by x' has no effect. If u!=0, normalize |u|=1. Replacing
x by x' moves the threshold in every integer fiber by at most |x-x'|. The
volume of the intervening slab in any fiber is at most
kappa_(d-1) R_*^(d-1) |x-x'|, by integration of perpendicular sections of the
containing ball. Use kappa_0=1 when d=1. Summing over P proves that the
unnormalized halfspace depth at fixed integer z is Lipschitz in x with the
uniform constant

    |P| kappa_(d-1) R_*^(d-1).

This estimate covers all oblique halfspaces, even when a is unbounded; the
vertical halfspaces contribute zero change. Total variation changes the
infimum over halfspaces at any fixed candidate by at most the total
variation difference of the measures. Hence if x_j in K_z^j converges to
x in K_z^infinity, the depths converge after normalization by M_j.

Each maximum exists by continuity on finitely many compact fibers. For an
upper limit of the maxima, choose maximizers and take a subsequence with a
constant integer coordinate and converging continuous coordinates. For a
lower limit, approximate a limiting maximizer in its fixed fiber using
Hausdorff convergence. The preceding estimates give equality of the upper
and lower limits, proving continuity of the normalized maximum depth.

This supplies a rigorous compactness and extremum-attainment tool on the
fixed nonhollow projection class. It supplies no reduction to this class
from arbitrary projections and no proof of the OC constant.

## 6. Consequence for a fixed nonhollow projection

Suppose P spans R^n and has a specified interior integer point z_0. Consider
all actual convex fiber families over P that have positive total mixed
d-volume; other fibers are allowed to be lower-dimensional. Then the central
fiber K_(z_0) is automatically full-dimensional: the positive barycentric
weights of Section 2 show that it contains a translated positive multiple
of any positive-volume fiber.

Normalize its volume to one, then apply the determinant-one maps above. The
resulting families are precompact; every limit still has that central unit
volume and exactly the same projection P. The actual-fiber property is
closed. Hence, by continuity of maximized normalized depth, its infimum over
this entire fixed-P class is attained. No lower volume bounds on the remaining
fibers are necessary for this attainment assertion.

This is an attainment statement only for one fixed P. It does not make the
collection of all possible integer projections compact, does not control
sequences in which P changes, and does not cover hollow projections.
